analysis.investment_thesis: Eureka Forbes owns the dominant Aquaguard brand with a virtually debt-free balance sheet, but at 47x P/E and a dismal 3.71% ROE, the market is pricing in a future far rosier than the numbers currently justify. I will not pay this price for a business earning ₹164 Cr on ₹4,520 Cr of equity.
key_strengths: Fortress balance sheet — Debt/Equity of just 0.02, with borrowings shrinking from ₹256 Cr (2022) to ₹91 Cr (2025)
Aquaguard brand moat in water purification with 59% gross margins signalling strong services/AMC revenue mix
Consistently positive and growing free cash flow: ₹167 Cr → ₹169 Cr → ₹190 Cr over last 3 years
key_risks: ROE of 3.71% and ROCE of 5.07% are unacceptable — earning just ₹164 Cr on ₹4,520 Cr equity means the capital base is deeply underemployed
Valuation is punishing: P/E of 47x versus my comfort ceiling of 20x; FCF yield of ~2% (₹190 Cr FCF / ₹9,319 Cr market cap) offers no margin of safety
Revenue growth from 2023–2025 is only ~8% CAGR (₹2,085 Cr → ₹2,437 Cr), insufficient to justify a premium multiple
red_flags: Bloated equity base (₹4,520 Cr) relative to revenue (₹2,437 Cr) likely reflects acquisition goodwill from the Shapoorji Pallonji restructuring — real capital efficiency is obscured
Operating margin of 7.97% is at the very floor of acceptable; any volume pressure or input cost spike could compress it further
2021 data (₹8 Cr revenue, ₹7 Cr assets) reveals this is a restructured/demerged entity — full business track record under current ownership is less than 4 years
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Eureka Forbes is built around a genuinely strong consumer franchise — Aquaguard is a household name, the AMC-driven recurring revenue model explains the 59% gross margin, and the near-zero debt is exactly the kind of balance sheet I respect. Operating cash flow has grown steadily from ₹181 Cr to ₹246 Cr in three years, and the company has visibly improved net profit from ₹26 Cr to ₹164 Cr over the same period. These are real positives. The promoter stake at 62.6% is acceptable, and the debt trajectory is moving in the right direction.

However, the numbers fail my fundamental tests at today's price. A 3.71% ROE is not a consumer business moat story — it is a capital allocation problem. The equity base of ₹4,520 Cr sitting above a business generating ₹164 Cr in profits means every rupee of shareholder equity is earning less than a fixed deposit. At 47x earnings, the market has already priced in years of perfect execution, leaving no room for error. I need at least 15–18% ROE before I get interested, and I need to buy at 15–20x earnings, not 47x. I will watch this business — if the ROE improves toward 12%+ as profits scale against a stable equity base, and if the price corrects to below 25x, this becomes worth revisiting.
